nodes.label: LTEE Cit+ emergence and Cit++ expansion
nodes.summary: Leon et al. (2018) describe emergence of citrate utilization in the Ara−3 LTEE population after 31,500 generations and descendants fully exploiting citrate by 33,000 generations.

nodes.label: CitT duplication fitness in early LTEE Cit+ isolate
nodes.summary: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 2.2% competitive fitness advantage associated with the citT-activating duplication by comparing early Cit+ isolate ZDB564 with its Cit− revertant ZDB706.

nodes.label: Weak ancestral fitness benefit of aerobic citT activation
nodes.summary: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 1.0% fitness advantage for the engineered Cit+ activation in ancestral LTEE strain REL606, with weak statistical support (one-tailed P = 0.033; n = 12).

nodes.label: Deleterious citT activation in evolved genetic backgrounds
nodes.summary: Leon et al. (2018) reported that activating citT reduced competitive fitness in 11 of 23 tested evolved pre-Cit+ clones, including five with reductions greater than 20%.

nodes.label: Negative Cit+ activation effect in intermediate Ara−3 phylogeny
nodes.summary: Leon et al. (2018) estimated a −5.4% fitness effect (interval −7.2% to −3.6%) for citT activation in the intermediate pre-Cit+ lineage group represented by ZDB425, ZDB458 and ZDB464.

nodes.label: Late positive Cit+ activation effect in Ara−3 phylogeny
nodes.summary: Leon et al. (2018) estimated a +2.4% fitness effect (95% interval +1.4% to +3.4%) in a later fully potentiated pre-Cit+ lineage group containing ZDB19 and ZDB13 from as early as 29,000 generations.

nodes.label: Ecological potentiation test in evolved generation-31,000 Ara−3 population mixture
nodes.summary: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 0.9% Cit+ fitness advantage when competing engineered ZDB706 variants at low frequency within the generation-31,000 LTEE population and reported no support for an ecological-potentiation advantage.

nodes.label: Loss of detectable Cit− lineage in Ara−3 samples
nodes.summary: Turner et al. (2015) detected the Ara−3 Cit− genotype and phenotype through 43,500 LTEE generations but not in samples from 44,000 generations onward.

nodes.label: Cit− persisted through 40 reconstructed evolution replays
nodes.summary: Turner et al. (2015) found Cit− persistence in all 20 replay populations from generation 43,500 and all 20 from generation 40,000 after 500 generations, plus one generation-43,000 replay propagated for 2,500 generations.

nodes.label: Reinvasion of a 50,000-generation Cit+ population
nodes.summary: Turner et al. (2015) observed that a generation-43,000 Cit− clone reinvaded the generation-50,000 Ara−3 population, reaching about 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, roughly an order of magnitude below final Cit− densities in the other treatments.

nodes.label: Turner extinction cause unresolved; random-catastrophe proposal
nodes.summary: Turner et al. (2015) stated that the Ara−3 Cit− lineage extinction cause remained unknown, rejected their initial ongoing Cit+ adaptation explanation, and proposed an unidentified rare perturbation as a possible cause rather than an observed event.

canonical_record.label: LTEE Cit+ emergence and Cit++ expansion
canonical_record.summary: Leon et al. (2018) describe emergence of citrate utilization in the Ara−3 LTEE population after 31,500 generations and descendants fully exploiting citrate by 33,000 generations.

assertions.statement: Leon et al. (2018) describe emergence of citrate utilization in the Ara−3 LTEE population after 31,500 generations and descendants fully exploiting citrate by 33,000 generations.

scope.population: One of twelve LTEE E. coli populations, Ara−3
scope.assumptions: Historical timeline recounted by Leon et al. from earlier LTEE studies; distinction between rudimentary Cit+ and refined Cit++.
scope.uncertainty: No assertion that the first cell carrying Cit+ was directly observed or that changes occurred in the other eleven populations.

support.quote:
After 31,500 generations, a mutant in one of the LTEE populations, designated Ara
−
3, evolved the ability to utilize citrate as a carbon source. Descendants of this mutant that were able to fully exploit this additional carbon source evolved by 33,000 generations and dominated thereafter

canonical_record.label: CitT duplication fitness in early LTEE Cit+ isolate
canonical_record.summary: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 2.2% competitive fitness advantage associated with the citT-activating duplication by comparing early Cit+ isolate ZDB564 with its Cit− revertant ZDB706.

assertions.statement: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 2.2% competitive fitness advantage associated with the citT-activating duplication by comparing early Cit+ isolate ZDB564 with its Cit− revertant ZDB706.

scope.population: ZDB564 and its ZDB706 revertant in direct DM-medium competition
scope.time: Earliest Cit+ isolate ZDB564 from generation 31,500; tests reported in 2018
scope.assumptions: Competitive co-culture, controlled neutral arabinose-marker variants; duplication differs between compared strains.
scope.uncertainty: The paper describes a small measured advantage for these strains, not a general advantage in all genetic backgrounds.

support.quote:
When competing ZDB564 and ZDB706, we found a slight fitness advantage of 2.2% for the presence of the
citT
-activating duplication in ZDB564

canonical_record.label: Weak ancestral fitness benefit of aerobic citT activation
canonical_record.summary: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 1.0% fitness advantage for the engineered Cit+ activation in ancestral LTEE strain REL606, with weak statistical support (one-tailed P = 0.033; n = 12).

assertions.statement: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 1.0% fitness advantage for the engineered Cit+ activation in ancestral LTEE strain REL606, with weak statistical support (one-tailed P = 0.033; n = 12).

scope.population: Ancestral REL606 LTEE E. coli with P_rnk-citT chromosomal knock-in versus null cassette
scope.assumptions: Knock-in mimic of evolved activation, not spontaneous appearance of the authentic tandem duplication in ancestor.
scope.uncertainty: Effect near assay resolution; authors explicitly describe relatively weak support.
scope.units: relative fitness percent; P-value; observations n

support.quote:
We found a slight fitness benefit of 1.0% for the Cit
+
mutation (
Fig 1B
). This effect size is near the limit for the smallest differences that can be distinguished in these types of competitive fitness assays, resulting in relatively weak support for the hypothesis that there was any fitness advantage at all for the REL606 variant with the P
rnk
-citT
module relative to the one with the null module (one-tailed
t
-test,
P
= 0.033,
n
= 12).

canonical_record.label: Deleterious citT activation in evolved genetic backgrounds
canonical_record.summary: Leon et al. (2018) reported that activating citT reduced competitive fitness in 11 of 23 tested evolved pre-Cit+ clones, including five with reductions greater than 20%.

assertions.statement: Leon et al. (2018) reported that activating citT reduced competitive fitness in 11 of 23 tested evolved pre-Cit+ clones, including five with reductions greater than 20%.

scope.population: 23 additional evolved pre-Cit+ LTEE Ara−3 clones assayed with citT activation and control cassettes
scope.time: Strains sampled at multiple pre-Cit+ generations; tests reported 2018
scope.assumptions: The 23 are sampled isolates, not all LTEE genotypes or all twelve populations.
scope.uncertainty: Fitness reduction depends on genetic background; one-tailed bootstrap tests P<0.05 for reported comparisons.
scope.quantifiers: 11/23 strains disadvantage; 5 strains greater than 20% disadvantage

support.quote:
Unexpectedly, the Cit
−
variant outcompeted the Cit
+
variant for the 11 remaining strains of the 23 we tested (one-tailed bootstrap test,
P
< 0.05). The actualizing step needed for subsequently evolving full citrate utilization (Cit
++
) would have been effectively blocked if it occurred in these strain backgrounds; they are ‘anti-potentiated’. For five of these strains, activating
citT
expression was extremely detrimental, decreasing competitive fitness by >20% (one-tailed bootstrap test,
P
< 0.05).

canonical_record.label: Negative Cit+ activation effect in intermediate Ara−3 phylogeny
canonical_record.summary: Leon et al. (2018) estimated a −5.4% fitness effect (interval −7.2% to −3.6%) for citT activation in the intermediate pre-Cit+ lineage group represented by ZDB425, ZDB458 and ZDB464.

assertions.statement: Leon et al. (2018) estimated a −5.4% fitness effect (interval −7.2% to −3.6%) for citT activation in the intermediate pre-Cit+ lineage group represented by ZDB425, ZDB458 and ZDB464.

scope.population: Phylogenetically grouped pre-Cit+ Ara−3 isolates ZDB425, ZDB458, and ZDB464
scope.time: Intermediate lineage samples, including generation 10,000 ZDB425 and generation 20,000 ZDB458
scope.assumptions: Fitness effect pooled in a phylogenetically selected group; private mutations and uncertain changes on the ancestral line limit attribution.
scope.uncertainty: Authors do not rule out additional changes in fitness effect during the 10,000–20,000-generation interval.

support.quote:
It was deleterious to evolve Cit
+
in an earlier, intermediate set of isolates composed of ZDB425, ZDB458, and ZDB464 with an estimated fitness effect of –5.4% [–7.2%, –3.6%].

ZDB425 at 10,000 generations and ZDB458 at 20,000 generations have only one and two ‘private’ mutations not shared with the main pre-Cit
+
lineage, respectively, though we cannot rule out that other changes in the impact of
citT
activation may have occurred on the main line of descent within this interval.

canonical_record.label: Late positive Cit+ activation effect in Ara−3 phylogeny
canonical_record.summary: Leon et al. (2018) estimated a +2.4% fitness effect (95% interval +1.4% to +3.4%) in a later fully potentiated pre-Cit+ lineage group containing ZDB19 and ZDB13 from as early as 29,000 generations.

assertions.statement: Leon et al. (2018) estimated a +2.4% fitness effect (95% interval +1.4% to +3.4%) in a later fully potentiated pre-Cit+ lineage group containing ZDB19 and ZDB13 from as early as 29,000 generations.

scope.population: Late pre-Cit+ Ara−3 lineage group including ZDB19, ZDB13, and the ZDB706 reference background
scope.time: As early as 29,000 generations; assays reported in 2018
scope.assumptions: Fitness impact of activating citT in a specified related group, not a whole-population estimate.
scope.uncertainty: Positive group estimate does not establish causal genetic variants or guarantee the evolutionary success of a Cit+ lineage.

support.quote:
Proceeding backward in the tree from the earliest known Cit
+
isolate (ZDB564), two earlier clones (ZDB19 and ZDB13) from as early as 29,000 generations are as fully potentiated as the key Cit
−
revertant (ZDB706). The overall fitness effect of evolving Cit
+
in this group was +2.4% [+1.4%, +3.4%] (95% confidence interval).

canonical_record.label: Ecological potentiation test in evolved generation-31,000 Ara−3 population mixture
canonical_record.summary: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 0.9% Cit+ fitness advantage when competing engineered ZDB706 variants at low frequency within the generation-31,000 LTEE population and reported no support for an ecological-potentiation advantage.

assertions.statement: Leon et al. (2018) measured a 0.9% Cit+ fitness advantage when competing engineered ZDB706 variants at low frequency within the generation-31,000 LTEE population and reported no support for an ecological-potentiation advantage.

scope.population: Engineered Cit+ and Cit− variants of ZDB706 in a background of the full generation-31,000 Ara−3 LTEE population
scope.assumptions: Cit+ and Cit− variants started equally and together formed about 1% of population mixture; comparison with direct variant competitions.
scope.uncertainty: The authors report marginal difference from pairwise competition (two-tailed P=0.053), not a definitive exclusion of all ecological effects.
scope.units: relative fitness percent; P-value; frequency percent

support.quote:
The Cit
+
and Cit
−
variants were mixed together equally and added such that they comprised ~1% of the cells in a mixture with the evolved population sample.

In this context, the Cit
+
strain had a 0.9% fitness advantage over the Cit
−
strain, which was less than and only marginally different from the result when the two strains were competed versus one another normally (two-tailed
t
-test,
P
= 0.053). Thus, we find no support for the ecological potentiation hypothesis.

canonical_record.label: Loss of detectable Cit− lineage in Ara−3 samples
canonical_record.summary: Turner et al. (2015) detected the Ara−3 Cit− genotype and phenotype through 43,500 LTEE generations but not in samples from 44,000 generations onward.

assertions.statement: Turner et al. (2015) detected the Ara−3 Cit− genotype and phenotype through 43,500 LTEE generations but not in samples from 44,000 generations onward.

scope.population: Frozen Ara−3 LTEE samples surveyed by genotype-specific PCR and phenotypic colony screens
scope.time: 43,500 to 44,000 generations and later archived samples
scope.assumptions: PCR and colony phenotype assays applied to sampled material; disappearance inferred from detection limits.
scope.uncertainty: Absence of detectable signal is not a guarantee that no Cit− cell survived anywhere below assay sensitivity.

support.quote:
The PCR assay for the presence of the Cit
−
genotype produced clear bands of the expected size at all time points up to and including 43,500 generations (
Fig 1
). At 44,000 generations and beyond, we did not observe any amplification. Phenotypic screens also indicated that the Cit
−
lineage went extinct between 43,500 and 44,000 generations. Cit
−
cells were detected through 43,500 generations in all cultures, but not at any later time point.

canonical_record.label: Cit− persisted through 40 reconstructed evolution replays
canonical_record.summary: Turner et al. (2015) found Cit− persistence in all 20 replay populations from generation 43,500 and all 20 from generation 40,000 after 500 generations, plus one generation-43,000 replay propagated for 2,500 generations.

assertions.statement: Turner et al. (2015) found Cit− persistence in all 20 replay populations from generation 43,500 and all 20 from generation 40,000 after 500 generations, plus one generation-43,000 replay propagated for 2,500 generations.

scope.population: 40 independently propagated Ara−3 replay cultures from frozen generation-43,500 and generation-40,000 populations; one additional from 43,000
scope.time: 500 replay generations in each of 40 populations; 2,500 in one additional replay
scope.assumptions: Standard LTEE conditions and genotype-specific PCR; frozen source populations may not reproduce any unrecorded environment perturbation.
scope.uncertainty: Zero extinctions in replays challenges repeatability under those conditions, not all hypothetical competitive-exclusion mechanisms.
scope.quantifiers: 20+20 replays without Cit− loss; one 2,500-generation extension

support.quote:
Twenty replicate populations founded from the 43,500-generation population sample evolved for 500 generations under the standard LTEE conditions. PCR assays showed that the Cit
−
clade persisted in all 20 cases through the end of the experiment. The Cit
−
lineage also persisted in all 20 control populations founded from the 40,000-generation population sample, and in the population founded from the 43,000-generation population sample that evolved for 2,500 generations.

canonical_record.label: Reinvasion of a 50,000-generation Cit+ population
canonical_record.summary: Turner et al. (2015) observed that a generation-43,000 Cit− clone reinvaded the generation-50,000 Ara−3 population, reaching about 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, roughly an order of magnitude below final Cit− densities in the other treatments.

assertions.statement: Turner et al. (2015) observed that a generation-43,000 Cit− clone reinvaded the generation-50,000 Ara−3 population, reaching about 3 × 10^5 cells/mL, roughly an order of magnitude below final Cit− densities in the other treatments.

scope.population: Generation-43,000 Cit− clone added to frozen generation-50,000 Cit+ whole-population sample under LTEE competition conditions
scope.assumptions: Invasion refers to tested archived mixed culture and the added clone; low and high inoculation conditions were averaged.
scope.uncertainty: Observed coexistence in short assay does not prove permanent ecological coexistence or identify the extinction cause.
scope.quantifiers: 3 × 10^5 cells/mL; about 10-fold lower; mean across two starting densities

support.quote:
When added to the 50,000-generation population—more than 6,000 generations after the extinction of the Cit
−
lineage—the 43,000-generation Cit
−
clone could still invade the Cit
+
population (
Fig 2A
). However, the final Cit
−
population size was an order of magnitude lower (3 x 10
5

−
cells in any other treatment (

canonical_record.label: Turner extinction cause unresolved; random-catastrophe proposal
canonical_record.summary: Turner et al. (2015) stated that the Ara−3 Cit− lineage extinction cause remained unknown, rejected their initial ongoing Cit+ adaptation explanation, and proposed an unidentified rare perturbation as a possible cause rather than an observed event.

assertions.statement: Turner et al. (2015) stated that the Ara−3 Cit− lineage extinction cause remained unknown, rejected their initial ongoing Cit+ adaptation explanation, and proposed an unidentified rare perturbation as a possible cause rather than an observed event.

scope.population: Ara−3 Cit− ecological lineage extinction between generation 43,500 and 44,000
scope.time: Authors’ 2015 interpretation of extinction and replay results
scope.assumptions: Reasoning combines failed replay repeatability, reinvasion, population-size argument, and hypothetical perturbation, not direct observation of a catastrophe.
scope.uncertainty: Environmental shock, soap residue, or water problem are hypotheses, not established mechanisms; complex alternatives discussed in paper are not proven impossible.
scope.quantifiers: One lineage extinction; possible rare event

support.quote:
The cause of the Cit
−
lineage’s extinction remains unknown. We have rejected our initial hypothesis that on-going adaptation of the Cit
+
bacteria caused the extinction. A purely stochastic extinction of the Cit
−
lineage is also extremely unlikely.

We propose, therefore, that the cause of the Cit
−
extinction was a “random catastrophe”, that is, a large, rare event that reduced the size of the Ara–3 population as a whole or, at least, the Cit
−
lineage within it. We do not know the nature of this random catastrophe, but it could have been some unusual variation in laboratory conditions, such as soap residue in a flask or a problem with the deionized water used to make the culture medium.
